discovery.note: Discovered with the new spectroscope from two deep red lines in mineral water and lepidolite.

nameOrigin: Latin rubidus, deep red, for its spectral lines.

radioactive.note: 27.83% of natural rubidium; used in rubidium-strontium dating of rocks.

elementalForm.description: Each rubidium atom gives its single 5s electron to a very weak metallic electron sea; the metal melts at 39 °C.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in stars.
appearance: Very soft, silvery-white metal that ignites in air.
summary: Rubidium is a very reactive alkali metal. Its atoms are the workhorses of atomic clocks and the first Bose-Einstein condensate.
uses: Rubidium atomic clocks (in GPS and phone networks)
facts: The first Bose-Einstein condensate, in 1995, was made from rubidium-87 atoms.
biology: None known; the body treats it much like potassium.
hazards: Ignites in air and reacts explosively with water.

discovery.note: Recognized in the mineral strontianite; isolated by Humphry Davy in 1808.

nameOrigin: Strontian, a village in Scotland where its ore was found.

radioactive.note: A dangerous fission product that collects in bones.

elementalForm.description: Strontium atoms share two 5s electrons each in a metallic electron sea.

originNote: Mostly made by slow neutron capture in aging stars.
appearance: Soft, silvery metal that yellows in air.
summary: Strontium is a reactive alkaline-earth metal best known for the brilliant red of fireworks. Strontium optical lattice clocks are among the most precise instruments ever built.
facts: Strontium clocks would lose less than a second in the age of the universe.
biology: Not essential; it can replace calcium in bones.
hazards: Stable strontium is of low toxicity; radioactive Sr-90 is dangerous.

discovery.note: Found in a black mineral from the Ytterby quarry in Sweden.

nameOrigin: Ytterby, Sweden (which also gave names to ytterbium, terbium and erbium).

elementalForm.description: Yttrium contributes three valence electrons (5s2 4d1) to metallic bonding, like the lanthanides it resembles.

originNote: Made mostly by slow neutron capture in aging stars.
appearance: Silvery metal, fairly stable in air.
summary: Yttrium behaves much like the rare-earth elements. It is the Y in YBCO, a famous high-temperature superconductor, and in YAG lasers.
facts: Moon rocks brought back by Apollo were unusually rich in yttrium.

discovery.note: Found as an oxide in zircon; impure metal was isolated by Berzelius in 1824.

elementalForm.description: Zirconium contributes four valence electrons (5s2 4d2) to strong metallic bonding.

originNote: Made mostly by slow neutron capture in aging stars.
summary: Zirconium barely absorbs neutrons and resists corrosion, so it clads the fuel rods in nuclear reactors. Zircon crystals are the oldest known pieces of Earth.
facts: Zircon crystals from Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old.
hazards: Low toxicity; fine powder can ignite.

discovery.note: Named columbium; confused with tantalum until Heinrich Rose separated them in 1844.

nameOrigin: Niobe, daughter of Tantalus in Greek myth, because it is so like tantalum.

elementalForm.description: Niobium (4d4 5s1) contributes five valence electrons to strong metallic bonding.

originNote: Made by neutron capture in several kinds of stars.
appearance: Grey metal that turns blue, green or violet when anodized.
summary: Niobium becomes superconducting at 9.2 K, the highest of any pure element at normal pressure. Niobium-titanium wire builds the magnets of MRI scanners and the Large Hadron Collider.
facts: About 90% of the world's niobium comes from Brazil.

discovery.note: Scheele showed molybdenite was not graphite; Peter Jacob Hjelm isolated the metal in 1781.

nameOrigin: Greek molybdos, lead, because its ore was confused with lead ore.

radioactive.note: Parent of technetium-99m for medical scans.

elementalForm.description: Molybdenum (4d5 5s1) shares six valence electrons; half-filled d orbitals give very strong metallic bonding and a melting point above 2,600 °C.

summary: Molybdenum is a hard, high-melting metal that strengthens steel. Nitrogen-fixing bacteria depend on a molybdenum enzyme to turn air into fertilizer.
uses: Catalysts for removing sulfur from fuels
facts: Nitrogenase, the enzyme that fixes nitrogen from air, contains molybdenum.
biology: Essential: part of several enzymes in plants, animals and bacteria.

discovery.note: Found in molybdenum foil bombarded in a cyclotron: the first element made artificially.

radioactive.note: Used in tens of millions of medical scans each year.

elementalForm.description: Technetium shares its seven valence electrons in metallic bonding, like its neighbors manganese and rhenium.

originNote: All its isotopes are radioactive; tiny traces form naturally in uranium ores, and red giant stars show technetium lines, proving stars make new elements.
summary: Technetium is the lightest element with no stable isotopes. Its metastable isotope technetium-99m is the most widely used medical imaging tracer.
facts: Mendeleev left a gap for it in 1871, but it was only made 66 years later.
biology: None; used only as a diagnostic tracer.

discovery.note: Isolated from platinum ore residues in Kazan.

elementalForm.description: Ruthenium shares its 4d and 5s electrons in a hard, strong metallic lattice.

originNote: Mostly made by rapid neutron capture in neutron-star mergers.
summary: Ruthenium is a rare, hard platinum-group metal. It makes electrical contacts wear-resistant and is used in important catalysts.
facts: Gottfried Osann reported it in 1827, but Claus was the first to prove it was a new element.
Thin films of ruthenium in an unusual tetragonal form were shown in 2018 to be magnetic at room temperature.
hazards: Ruthenium tetroxide is highly toxic and explosive.

discovery.note: Found in platinum ore dissolved in aqua regia.

nameOrigin: Greek rhodon, rose, for its rose-colored salts.

elementalForm.description: Rhodium (4d8 5s1) forms a dense, highly reflective metallic lattice.

originNote: Mostly made by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Rhodium is one of the rarest and most expensive metals. Most of it goes into car catalytic converters, where it breaks down nitrogen oxides.
facts: Rhodium has at times been the most expensive precious metal, over ten times the price of gold.
hazards: Low toxicity as metal; some compounds are harmful.

discovery.note: Found in platinum ore and first sold anonymously as 'new silver'.

nameOrigin: The asteroid Pallas, discovered a year earlier.

elementalForm.description: Palladium (4d10, with no 5s electron in the free atom) forms a metallic lattice that can soak up hundreds of times its own volume of hydrogen.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Palladium absorbs hydrogen like a sponge and is a superb catalyst. Its electron configuration, 4d10 with an empty 5s, is unique.
facts: Palladium can absorb up to about 900 times its own volume of hydrogen.

discovery.note: Mined since at least 3000 BCE in Anatolia.

nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon seolfor; symbol Ag from Latin argentum.

elementalForm.description: Silver (4d10 5s1) shares its single 5s electron in a very mobile electron sea, which gives it the highest electrical conductivity of any element.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Silver conducts electricity and heat better than any other element and reflects visible light best of all metals. Silver ions kill bacteria.
facts: Silver tarnish is silver sulfide, formed by sulfur compounds in the air.
biology: None; silver ions are toxic to microbes.
hazards: Low toxicity; long exposure can turn skin blue-grey (argyria).

discovery.note: Found as an impurity that colored zinc carbonate yellow.

radioactive.note: 12.22% of natural cadmium; a strong neutron absorber.

elementalForm.description: Cadmium shares its two 5s electrons; the full 4d shell stays out, so bonding is weak and cadmium melts at 321 °C.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
summary: Cadmium is a soft metal used in batteries, pigments and solar cells. It is highly toxic, so many of its uses are being phased out.
facts: Itai-itai disease in 1950s Japan was caused by cadmium-polluted rice.
biology: None in humans; one marine diatom uses a cadmium enzyme.
hazards: Toxic and carcinogenic; damages kidneys and bones.

discovery.note: Found from a brilliant indigo line in the spectrum of zinc ore.

nameOrigin: The indigo line in its spectrum.

elementalForm.description: Indium shares three valence electrons (5s2 5p1) in a soft metallic lattice.

bulk.structure: Body-centered tetragonal (a slightly stretched face-centered cell)
bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified face-centered cubic lattice.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Very soft, silvery metal that cries when bent.
summary: Indium is soft enough to scratch with a fingernail. Indium tin oxide forms the transparent, conductive layer in touchscreens and flat displays.
uses: Indium tin oxide for touchscreens and displays
facts: Bending an indium bar makes a high-pitched 'cry' as its crystals slip.
hazards: Inhaled indium compounds can harm the lungs.

discovery.note: Used since about 3500 BCE, mainly to make bronze.

nameOrigin: Anglo-Saxon tin; symbol Sn from Latin stannum.

elementalForm.description: White tin is metallic. Below 13 °C it can slowly change into grey tin, a brittle diamond-structure semiconductor where each atom shares pairs with four neighbors.

bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified close-packed lattice.

originNote: Made by slow and rapid neutron capture.
summary: Tin has ten stable isotopes, more than any other element. Mixed with copper it made bronze, and today it is mostly used in solder.
facts: Tin has 10 stable isotopes, the most of any element.
hazards: Metal is low-toxicity; organotin compounds are very toxic.

discovery.note: Stibnite (antimony sulfide) was used as eye makeup in ancient Egypt.

nameOrigin: Possibly Greek anti-monos, 'not alone'; symbol Sb from Latin stibium.

elementalForm.description: Like grey arsenic, each antimony atom shares pairs with three neighbors in puckered layers and keeps a lone pair; it conducts like a poor metal.

bulk.note: Drawn as a simplified distorted cubic net.

originNote: Made by rapid and slow neutron capture.
summary: Antimony is a brittle metalloid that, like water, expands slightly as it freezes, which made it valuable for casting sharp printing type.
facts: Ancient Egyptians used antimony sulfide as kohl eyeliner.
hazards: Toxic, similar to arsenic but milder.

discovery.note: Found in gold ore from Transylvania; named by Klaproth in 1798.

radioactive.note: 31.74% of natural tellurium: the slowest decay ever measured.

elementalForm.description: Tellurium is built from spiral chains, like grey selenium: each atom shares one pair with each chain neighbor and keeps two lone pairs.

originNote: Made almost entirely by rapid neutron capture.
summary: Tellurium is one of the rarest stable elements in the crust. Tellurium-128 decays so slowly that its half-life is more than 100 trillion times the age of the universe.
facts: People exposed to tellurium can get strong garlic-smelling breath.

discovery.note: Seen as violet vapor while making saltpeter from seaweed ash.

radioactive.note: Treats thyroid disease; a hazard in nuclear accidents.
Used in seed implants and lab assays.

elementalForm.description: Two iodine atoms share one electron pair and each keeps three lone pairs. Large, easily distorted I2 molecules attract each other enough to form a solid.

appearance: Shiny blue-black crystals that give off violet vapor.
summary: Iodine is a dark solid halogen that turns straight into violet vapor when warmed. Your thyroid needs it to make the hormones that control metabolism.
facts: Iodine deficiency is the world's most preventable cause of brain damage; iodized salt fixed it in many countries.
biology: Essential: part of the thyroid hormones thyroxine (T4) and T3.
hazards: Vapor irritates eyes and lungs; large doses are toxic.

discovery.note: Found in the last residues of evaporating liquid air.

elementalForm.description: Xenon has a full octet, but its outer electrons are far from the nucleus. Strongly electron-hungry atoms like fluorine and oxygen can pull them into bonds, forming compounds such as XeF2 and XeF4.

originNote: Made mostly by rapid neutron capture.
appearance: Colorless, very dense gas; glows blue-violet in a discharge.
summary: Xenon was the first noble gas found to form compounds, in 1962. Its bright arc light is used in film projectors and car headlights.
facts: Neil Bartlett's 1962 xenon compound overturned the idea that noble gases cannot react.
biology: None, though it acts as an anesthetic.
